title: Robust coexistence in competitive ecological communities

paper_content.abstract: Darwin already recognized that competition is fiercest among conspecifics, a principle that later made intraspecific competition central to ecological theory through concepts such as niche differentiation and limiting similarity. Beyond shaping coexistence, strong intraspecific competition can also stabilize community dynamics by ensuring that populations return to equilibrium after disturbance. Here we investigate a more fundamental question: how intraspecific competition influences the very existence of a steady state (feasibility) in large random ecological communities dominated by competition. We show that, in analogy with classical results on stability, there is a critical level of intraspecific competition above which a feasible steady state is guaranteed to exist. We derive a general expression for the probability of feasibility and prove that, asymptotically (as species number grows), the transition to stability occurs before the transition to feasibility with probability one. Thus, in large competitive communities, any feasible equilibrium is automatically stable. This ordering persists even when many species in the initial pool cannot coexist and extinctions occur: the dynamics prune the community, shifting feasibility and stability thresholds but never reversing their order. These results imply that large competitive communities generically converge to a globally stable equilibrium, making sustained oscillations or chaos unlikely—consistent with experimental observations.
paper_content.introduction:
The notions of intraspecific competition and population self-regulation play a central role in ecological theory, leading to foundational concepts such as limiting similarity and niche differentiation1–6. They also are crucial for coexistence: for example, May7 showed that ecological dynamics can be stabilized by imposing sufficiently strong intraspecific competition, and that for large systems with random species interactions the stability transition is universal (independent of the probability distribution used to model interactions) and sharp (always achieved at the same critical value of intraspecific competition). Importantly, the existence of an equilibrium (feasibility) is a necessary condition for coexistence. Further, results on stability can dramatically change when accounting for feasibility. The first contribution to this problem can be traced back to a response to May’s work on stability8, showing that in competitive Lotka-Volterra models with random interactions the probability of stability, conditioned on the presence of a feasible equilibrium, does increase, rather than decrease with system size. Since then, significant advances have been gradually accumulating in the literature9–15 (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 2). However, the progress on the study of feasibility has yet to match that reached for stability7,16–18. Here we show that accounting for feasibility is key to determining the expected dynamics of large competitive systems.

We compute the probability that a system would display a feasible equilibrium given its level of intraspecific competition, size, and the statistics on the random distribution of species interactions. We show that the transition to feasibility is universal, as for stability, but is not sharp—thereby extending, generalizing and refining previous results8,9,12,14,19–22. More importantly, we show that, in large competitive systems, when we increase the strength of intraspecific competition, the transition to stability precedes that to feasibility8,9,20. Therefore, in these large systems feasibility implies stability. This result holds even when the initial pool of species cannot coexist, and extinctions ensue. That is, during ecological dynamics, species extinctions will alter the values for the stability and feasibility thresholds, but not their ordering. Differently from May, who focused on local asymptotic stability of an equilibrium, here we consider the stronger criterion of global stability—robust coexistence in which populations rebound from any perturbation short of extinction.

Overall, these findings have far-reaching implications for the ecological dynamics of large random competitive ecosystems. They rule out coexistence through limit cycles or chaos23,24, and instead indicate that the community dynamics converge to a highly-robust equilibrium, such that (1) any perturbation short of extinction would be buffered, (2) the community resists invasions, and (3) it can be assembled from the ground up25,26.

Stability and feasibility thresholds
We consider the Generalized Lotka-Volterra27–30 (GLV) model for n interacting populations:



where intrinsic growth rates r i are organized in the vector r, and interactions A ij in the matrix A. We say that Eq. (1) has a feasible (i.e., biologically attainable) equilibrium whenever there is a x⋆ > 0 such that x_ i = 0 for all populations, and that such a feasible equilibrium is asymptotically stable if dynamics return to it following a perturbation.
Following May7, we model A as the sum of two matrices, A = αI + B, where B collects the inter-specific interactions (B ij, i≠j). I is the identity random matrix, and α ≥ 0 the intraspecific competition in the system, assumed to be the same for all species (relaxing this assumption does not change the results, see Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 9).
Now we consider increasing α from zero to an arbitrary large positive value, and track the effects of this change on coexistence. We denote α S as the level of intraspecific competition that is sufficient to guarantee the (global) stability of an equilibrium (Methods, and Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3). Importantly, for any α ≥ α S stability is maintained, i.e., once surpassed this threshold, dynamics always converge to a globally stable equilibrium. Here we ask whether, in analogy to stability, there exist a critical level α F that a) guarantees the existence of a positive equilibrium, and b) further increasing α ≥ α F retains the feasibility of the equilibrium. In particular, we want to probe the relationship between α F and α S.
We start with a toy example (Fig. 1, n = 6, see Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Fig. 3 for an example with two populations), illustrating the effect of increasing α on feasibility and stability. We first sample a baseline interaction matrix B, and compute the thresholds for stability, α S, and feasibility, α F (Methods, and Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3, and Supplementary Note 2, Sec. 4), marked in Fig. 1 with green and yellow triangles, respectively. We then construct three interaction matrices A that differ only in their intraspecific competition values, α I, α II, and α III (Fig. 1). For each system, we integrate the dynamics in Eq. (1) from two different initial conditions (Fig. 1 bottom panels, solid vs. dashed lines), revealing three qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes.
System I (Fig. 1, left) undergoes extinctions and displays alternative stable states, indicating that the coexistence equilibrium is not feasible, and the resulting sub-community equilibrium is not globally stable (indeed, neither stability nor feasibility thresholds have been surpassed, since α I < α S < α F). System II (Fig. 1, middle), also displays extinctions (as there is no feasible equilibrium), but starting from different initial conditions no longer leads to different outcomes, because the equilibrium of the sub-community is globally stable (α S < α II < α F, and see Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3). Finally, system III (Fig. 1, right), exhibits all populations coexisting stably (α S < α F < α III). From this single realization, we can see that stability is achieved before feasibility. Next, we show that this is the case for large random ecological communities (but see Supplementary Note 2, Sec. 3 for results on small or arbitrary competitive systems).

Feasibility implies robust coexistence almost surely
As long as populations are statistically equivalent (i.e., there is no a priori structure making some populations behave differently from the rest), the distribution of the equilibrium values, y⋆, has always the same mean and correlation structure (Methods). Moreover, when n is large, we can assume the components of y⋆ to be approximately normally distributed9 and uncorrelated (“Methods”, and Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 7). Then, the probability of feasibility can be taken as the product of the probabilities that each component is positive, and can thus be written as the cumulative distribution function of a standard normal distribution, raised to the nth power (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 7):



Substituting this expression into Eq. (3), we obtain an extremely accurate analytical approximation of the probability of feasibility (Fig. 3, black curves): the probability p F(α) is vanishingly small when α = 0 (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 3), and increases smoothly to 1 with increasing α. Eq. (4) shows that the details of the distribution of interactions (Fig. 3, linetypes), once accounted for the correlation (Fig. 3, colors), are irrelevant when the system is large. This means that asymptotically, the curve describing the probability of feasibility is universal. Interestingly, exactly as a negative correlation between interaction strengths improves the chance of stability16, it also increases the probability of feasibility21. Contrary to current expectations14, the effect of the pairwise correlation ρ on the probability of feasibility remains significant for large systems (n = 1000 in Fig. 3). Additionally, the transition to feasibility also remains smooth compared to stability (Fig. 3, and Supplementary Fig. 10, see Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 8 for a detailed discussion) for large systems.
Importantly, our calculations show that for large systems the amount of self-regulation required for feasibility is high enough (i.e., α S < α F) to yield global stability (as argued before9,14,20,32,33). Then, a feasible system will be stable with probability 1, and thus p F(α) measures the probability of coexistence for a large, random competitive system. These results have profound implications for dynamics. Competitive GLV systems can give rise to any type of dynamics, including limit cycles (when n≥3) and chaos (n≥4)23,24. Importantly, however, non-equilibrium coexistence still requires the existence of a feasible equilibrium25. But we have seen that feasibility generically implies global stability, and therefore non-equilibrium coexistence is precluded.
When the system is not feasible, extinctions will ensue, pruning the original pool of species to a subsystem with different thresholds for feasibility and stability (Fig. 2c). As such, in principle, any type of dynamics could be observed. Next, we show that, despite the change in values of α S and α F caused by extinctions, the ordering α S < α F is maintained almost surely, provided that n is large. As a result, dynamics still converge to stable equilibria even when feasibility is not attained for the initial species pool.

Robust coexistence emerges through community dynamics
So far, we have investigated how coexistence is affected by increasing α. However, intraspecific competition models the effects of a species on itself. As such, when species are lost to extinction, the level of intraspecific competition should not be affected: the coefficients on the diagonal do not change when the matrix is pruned of the populations that have gone extinct. Thus, we turn our attention to a pool of n populations where we fix α < α S < α F (analogous to system I in Fig. 1), and consider “top-down assembly” (where all the species in the pool are introduced in the environment at the same time, Fig. 4a). Since we are below the feasibility threshold, some populations go extinct and, as a result, α F and α S changes (both values depend on n; Fig. 2c). We re-compute their values every time an extinction occurs (plotted in Fig. 4b), and find that their initial ordering is maintained throughout the dynamics until the system converges to a stable equilibrium after ecological dynamics have elapsed. Furthermore, we show (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 12) that the same equilibrium can be achieved via “bottom-up assembly”, through successive invasions26.
To confirm that these observations are a generic feature, we plot the ratio α F/α S when we run the same simulation in the previous example for many draws of random systems with the same characteristics (Fig. 4c). We see that the ratio is kept above one, implying that the relationship α S < α F is maintained throughout the dynamics for all the simulations. This shows that, with high probability, the dynamical outcome of large random competitive systems is always the same: a sub-set of the species pool will coexist robustly at an equilibrium that is characterized by α S < α F < α; the equilibrium is stable, and the last few populations to go extinct (if started in phase I), or all the extinct populations (if started in phase II) cannot re-invade the system.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript addresses a theoretical question whether feasible equilibria in large random competitive ecological systems are also dynamically stable. Based on analytical and numerical investigations of random matrix models, the authors concluded that feasibility implied stability in large systems governed by Lotka–Volterra dynamics with random interactions. The central claim is that the transition to dynamical stability consistently precedes the transition to feasibility, thus any feasible equilibrium is necessarily stable. These results provide a plausible explanation for the empirical observations in nature that communities of organisms interacting primarily through competition—such as species at the same trophic level—often exhibit stable equilibria, whereas sustained cycles and chaotic dynamics are more commonly associated with predator-prey systems or structured populations.
We found these results mathematically elegant and conceptually important. The analytical framework and insights offered here contribute to bridging ecological theories and observations, and the paper shall stimulate further research on the mechanisms underlying ecological stability. However, we have several concerns about the presentation, generality, and robustness of the results.
(1) The definition of stability needs to be further clarified. The ecological literature covers a broad set of different definitions of stability (local stability, resistance, recovery, variability, etc.), therefore it is important to clarify the meaning of ‘stability’ in the introduction as early as possible. Reading the paper, we had been thinking about ‘local stability’, but later it turned out to be ‘global stability’ after reading Fig. 1 and line 71. We believe that it is important to clarify in the Introduction which measure of stability will be focused on, why this measure is chosen (from the broad set, as well as between global vs. local stability), how they are defined and quantified, etc. In this regard, the authors may incorporate some general discussion form the supplementary materials explaining local and global stability.
(2) The paper included many arguments that was presented as general conclusions (e.g., L28, L93, L139, L172), which however – to the best of our understanding – hold only under certain contexts. For instance, in the abstract the statement “feasible systems will necessarily be stable” (line 28) was presented as a strong conclusion, but clearly it holds only under the study context using large competitive systems with random interaction strengths. Even in this context, the argument was supported primarily by asymptotic approximations and simulations, and neither the main text nor the appendix provided formal mathematical proofs establishing that α_S<α_F holds for all random matrices within the model class. Our preliminary simulations revealed counterexamples (i.e., feasible but unstable equilibria) even for n=50. So we recommend to be more cautious with conclusions, perhaps – feasibility implies stability with high probability in large random systems. Similarly, the main text and figure captions included quite a number of strong arguments with “always” “invariably” and “necessarily”. We recommend the authors to check throughout and avoid overstatement of the generality.
(3) The robustness of the results needs more examination. The paper did not provide sufficient information on the uncertainty involved in the simulations, such as confidence intervals, failure rates, or sensitivity bounds on the probability that feasibility implies stability (e.g., Figs. 2 & 3). Without such information, it is difficult to assess how robust the results are to variation in model settings. In particular, since the analytical solutions were obtained under the assumption of large communities with random interactions, we were wondering how large (cid:1) needs to be for the asymptotic results to reach a certain precision. The bottom-left panel in Fig. 2 provided some insights into this point, but an extended investigation would be useful for understanding the behaviors of the analytical solutions.
(4) Overall, the paper was quite brief, in terms of both results and discussion. This had made additional difficulties in the understanding of the paper. We recommended the authors to expand the manuscript by adding necessary explanations (e.g., context of analyses and conclusions, as explained above) and expanding the analyses by incorporating some results from the appendix. In particular, the main text presented the solutions mainly for feasibility, but little for the global stability. Is there a solution for the latter? If so, please provide them. If not, explain how were the thresholds obtained for stability in Figs. 1 & 2 (triangles)?
Moreover, the discussion should be substantially expanded to make connections to the literature. For instance, the recent paper by Hu et al. (2022) illustrated transitions from stable & feasible coexistence, to stable and unfeasible coexistence, and to fluctuating coexistence, as the number of species and average interaction strength increased. How do the findings in the current paper relate to and differ from Hu et al. (2022)? Also, many ecological models can produce scenarios where feasible equilibrium is not stable, such as the simplest two-species model with L-V type competition. How to reconcile the present study with these cases? Again, this needs to clarify the context of the results in this paper and reconcile them with broader models and patterns under different settings in the literature.
Minor comments:
Line 42. The statement “the stability of an equilibrium requires its existence (feasibility) in the first place” did not seem correct. As an example, Fig. 1 clearly showed the case (case II) where the community was infeasible but globally stable. Please specify the context where such argument should hold.
Line 104: vague arguments. What does it mean by ‘several transitions’? Please specify it if it is important, otherwise simplify the text.
Line 147: “the levels of intraspecific competition remain more or less constant over time” – why? Environmental fluctuations can certainly lead to variation in carrying capacity (K_i) and thus intraspecific competition (as defined here, i.e., α_ii=1/K_i). We felt that this argument argument was an assumption, but presented as a conclusion. This should be clarified.
Line 206: why ‘proportional to each other’? In the equation, y* also occur in the dominator, making it nonlinear.
Fig. 1: this is a very clear and interesting illustration. We think that such transitions could (though not necessarily always) occur already in L-V models with two competitors – that is, alternative stable states at low α_ii, deterministic exclusion at higher α_ii, and coexistence at very high α_ii. If so, this may help the readers to make the bridge to existing knowledge.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
I found the work presented in ‘Robust coexistence in ecological competitive communities’ very interesting, elegantly presented and quite exciting frankly. The authors demonstrate the significance of self-regulation as a mechanism for community persistence. In particular, the authors use random matrices to generate competitive ecological communities and show that increasing self-regulation (intra-specific competition) first achieves stability (fixed point equilibrium) and then feasibility (positive density of species at equilibrium). The order of stability being attained prior to feasibility (along the self-regulation gradient) implies that feasibility guarantees stability. An important corollary of this work is that competitive communities (that are large and have randomly distributed interaction strengths, a fundamental assumption and caveat) will have stable equilibria rather than non-equilibrium steady states.
I have one comment which touches upon the basic assumptions of this work. The authors use a single value for self-regulation, alpha, across species. Do I understand this correctly? This scenario would imply that all species share the same strength of self-regulation, while the strength of inter-specific interactions can vary. I wonder what would happen if there was a mean alpha for a matrix, rather than a fixed alpha for all species? How strongly would this impact the insights (obviously given different assumptions about the distribution of alpha’s)? Adding to this, what would happen if these alpha values were somehow correlated to the inter-specific interaction terms? For instance, a weak competitor with respect to other species, would presumably also have weak self-regulation to increase its survival chances. I understand that the authors simplified a very complex problem and I appreciate the value in such an approach. However, since the fundamental ecological parameter studied here is self-regulation, I would like the authors to explore the limitations of their simplifying assumptions regarding this parameter. Ultimately, it is important to understand the generality of their results to relaxing this assumption.
Besides this and to the extent that I was able to follow the mathematical analyses in the supplement, I found the justification of the results persuasive. Moreover, I liked how the manuscript was written; concisely, clearly and with a linearly progressing narrative. Overall, I really enjoyed reading this study and I would be happy to see it published so as to stimulate a debate in the broader community of interested ecologists.
My only regret was the absence of an ecological interpretation for the results, beyond the very obvious statements. For instance, as I mention in a comment below, I see some relation of certain results to niche theory; it would be very insightful to link the two. I believe there’s plenty of scope to expand on such nuances in the manuscript and I feel the authors would be doing ecologist readers a great service to expand on this aspect. Ultimately, given the journal and the style of the manuscript, I view this suggestion more as a ‘nice to have’ than a requirement for publication.
I have made more specific comments below, mostly for clarification purposes.
Title
Wouldn’t ‘Robust coexistence in competitive ecological communities’ sound better?
Abstract
The final sentence is quite strong. The absence of non-equilibrium steady states rests on certain assumptions (large, random interaction matrices). Consider toning down the absoluteness of the finding. Also, the authors could explain/expand on the notion of ‘robust’ coexistence (i.e., that this equilibrium cannot be invaded).
S1
l. 53 the authors can clarify the notion of ‘universal’ convergence to feasibility at this point so that it becomes easier to follow this line of reasoning.
l. 60 ‘resilient to any perturbation sort of extinction’: this statement is not very clear
S2
In fig1, add a brief description of the top panel, to make it immediately obvious that this refers to the interaction matrix entries, with the shade reflecting the magnitude of the parameters.
l. 83 ‘neither feasible’
S3
l.124-127 & eq. (4): it appears that as n increases, only the correlation (rho) will impact the variance and hence the probability of feasibility. If that is the case, I am not sure I understand l. 125, where I perceive the message as being that correlation (besides the mean and variance of the interaction matrix) is irrelevant.
l.131 e.g., what does P_F=0.5 mean for a community? In other words, what determines whether or not a community will be feasible? Are there other aspects of the interaction matrix distribution (higher moments?) whose consideration will make this outcome more definite? Is feasibility higher dimensional that stability and we require additional dimensions to make its transition sharp?
l. 142-144 I have a question which I am not sure I can present clearly, but I will try because I think there’s some value in answering it (if possible). We have the following information: for a given n and fixed alpha and rho, we can find the P_F (fig2, eqs. 3&4). If P_F<1, does this imply the community will ‘prune’ itself, to a lower n and attain P_F=1 (l. 143)? It would be interesting to seek a pattern linking these alpha’s to the ‘pruned’ community size n, for which P_F=1. If I understand correctly, it won’t matter whether these certainly feasible communities are the result of ‘pruning’ or bottom-up assembly. Perhaps, there are insights to be gained from a figure linking n to alpha such that P_F=1. Also, linked to this, I was wondering whether the slope of these curves (fig2) changes with n, i.e., does very large n lead to a sharp transition for instance?
fig2: the correlation in the interaction matrix can be seen as a proxy for specialisation, if I understand correctly. Positively correlated entries imply no trade-offs, while negative correlation indicate trade-offs and hence some kind of specialisation. This can be linked to the notion of the niche, which would seem to agree with the results: niche structure guarantees stability and facilitates feasibility (rho=-1), niche overlaps (rho=1) require much stronger self-regulation for the same outcomes. I think the manuscript would benefit significantly if such links between the mathematics and ecology were more pronounced and greater in number.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This revision substantially improves both rigor and readability. In particular, the revamped treatment around Fig. 2 now clearly articulates the relationships among feasibility and stability thresholds, contrasts the finite-n “multi-window” phenomenon with the large-n single transition, and maps these mathematical results onto ecological regimes (priority effects → deterministic exclusion → stable coexistence). The Discussion’s ecological interpretation is now well aligned with niche theory.
We have only one point to consider before publication. The extension to random diagonal terms (heterogeneous intraspecific competition) and the claim that the main qualitative transition persists for large n strengthen ecological realism. However, it remains unclear whether the number of transitions into and out of feasibility converges to one as community size increases when intraspecific competition is heterogeneous. If this “single-window” property is not robust to such heterogeneity (which should be the case in reality), conclusions that rely on a unique α_F may be fragile.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Darwin already recognized that competition is fiercest among conspecifics, a principle that later made intraspecific competition central to ecological theory through concepts such as niche differentiation and limiting similarity. Beyond shaping coexistence, strong intraspecific competition can also stabilize community dynamics by ensuring that populations return to equilibrium after disturbance. Here we investigate a more fundamental question: how intraspecific competition influences the very existence of a steady state (feasibility) in large random ecological communities dominated by competition. We show that, in analogy with classical results on stability, there is a critical level of intraspecific competition above which a feasible steady state is guaranteed to exist. We derive a general expression for the probability of feasibility and prove that, asymptotically (as species number grows), the transition to stability occurs before the transition to feasibility with probability one. Thus, in large competitive communities, any feasible equilibrium is automatically stable. This ordering persists even when many species in the initial pool cannot coexist and extinctions occur: the dynamics prune the community, shifting feasibility and stability thresholds but never reversing their order. These results imply that large competitive communities generically converge to a globally stable equilibrium, making sustained oscillations or chaos unlikely—consistent with experimental observations.

---

## Introduction

The notions of intraspecific competition and population self-regulation play a central role in ecological theory, leading to foundational concepts such as limiting similarity and niche differentiation1–6. They also are crucial for coexistence: for example, May7 showed that ecological dynamics can be stabilized by imposing sufficiently strong intraspecific competition, and that for large systems with random species interactions the stability transition is universal (independent of the probability distribution used to model interactions) and sharp (always achieved at the same critical value of intraspecific competition). Importantly, the existence of an equilibrium (feasibility) is a necessary condition for coexistence. Further, results on stability can dramatically change when accounting for feasibility. The first contribution to this problem can be traced back to a response to May’s work on stability8, showing that in competitive Lotka-Volterra models with random interactions the probability of stability, conditioned on the presence of a feasible equilibrium, does increase, rather than decrease with system size. Since then, significant advances have been gradually accumulating in the literature9–15 (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 2). However, the progress on the study of feasibility has yet to match that reached for stability7,16–18. Here we show that accounting for feasibility is key to determining the expected dynamics of large competitive systems.

We compute the probability that a system would display a feasible equilibrium given its level of intraspecific competition, size, and the statistics on the random distribution of species interactions. We show that the transition to feasibility is universal, as for stability, but is not sharp—thereby extending, generalizing and refining previous results8,9,12,14,19–22. More importantly, we show that, in large competitive systems, when we increase the strength of intraspecific competition, the transition to stability precedes that to feasibility8,9,20. Therefore, in these large systems feasibility implies stability. This result holds even when the initial pool of species cannot coexist, and extinctions ensue. That is, during ecological dynamics, species extinctions will alter the values for the stability and feasibility thresholds, but not their ordering. Differently from May, who focused on local asymptotic stability of an equilibrium, here we consider the stronger criterion of global stability—robust coexistence in which populations rebound from any perturbation short of extinction.

Overall, these findings have far-reaching implications for the ecological dynamics of large random competitive ecosystems. They rule out coexistence through limit cycles or chaos23,24, and instead indicate that the community dynamics converge to a highly-robust equilibrium, such that (1) any perturbation short of extinction would be buffered, (2) the community resists invasions, and (3) it can be assembled from the ground up25,26.

---

## Results

Stability and feasibility thresholds
We consider the Generalized Lotka-Volterra27–30 (GLV) model for n interacting populations:



where intrinsic growth rates r i are organized in the vector r, and interactions A ij in the matrix A. We say that Eq. (1) has a feasible (i.e., biologically attainable) equilibrium whenever there is a x⋆ > 0 such that x_ i = 0 for all populations, and that such a feasible equilibrium is asymptotically stable if dynamics return to it following a perturbation.
Following May7, we model A as the sum of two matrices, A = αI + B, where B collects the inter-specific interactions (B ij, i≠j). I is the identity random matrix, and α ≥ 0 the intraspecific competition in the system, assumed to be the same for all species (relaxing this assumption does not change the results, see Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 9).
Now we consider increasing α from zero to an arbitrary large positive value, and track the effects of this change on coexistence. We denote α S as the level of intraspecific competition that is sufficient to guarantee the (global) stability of an equilibrium (Methods, and Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3). Importantly, for any α ≥ α S stability is maintained, i.e., once surpassed this threshold, dynamics always converge to a globally stable equilibrium. Here we ask whether, in analogy to stability, there exist a critical level α F that a) guarantees the existence of a positive equilibrium, and b) further increasing α ≥ α F retains the feasibility of the equilibrium. In particular, we want to probe the relationship between α F and α S.
We start with a toy example (Fig. 1, n = 6, see Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Fig. 3 for an example with two populations), illustrating the effect of increasing α on feasibility and stability. We first sample a baseline interaction matrix B, and compute the thresholds for stability, α S, and feasibility, α F (Methods, and Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3, and Supplementary Note 2, Sec. 4), marked in Fig. 1 with green and yellow triangles, respectively. We then construct three interaction matrices A that differ only in their intraspecific competition values, α I, α II, and α III (Fig. 1). For each system, we integrate the dynamics in Eq. (1) from two different initial conditions (Fig. 1 bottom panels, solid vs. dashed lines), revealing three qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes.
System I (Fig. 1, left) undergoes extinctions and displays alternative stable states, indicating that the coexistence equilibrium is not feasible, and the resulting sub-community equilibrium is not globally stable (indeed, neither stability nor feasibility thresholds have been surpassed, since α I < α S < α F). System II (Fig. 1, middle), also displays extinctions (as there is no feasible equilibrium), but starting from different initial conditions no longer leads to different outcomes, because the equilibrium of the sub-community is globally stable (α S < α II < α F, and see Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3). Finally, system III (Fig. 1, right), exhibits all populations coexisting stably (α S < α F < α III). From this single realization, we can see that stability is achieved before feasibility. Next, we show that this is the case for large random ecological communities (but see Supplementary Note 2, Sec. 3 for results on small or arbitrary competitive systems).

Feasibility implies robust coexistence almost surely
As long as populations are statistically equivalent (i.e., there is no a priori structure making some populations behave differently from the rest), the distribution of the equilibrium values, y⋆, has always the same mean and correlation structure (Methods). Moreover, when n is large, we can assume the components of y⋆ to be approximately normally distributed9 and uncorrelated (“Methods”, and Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 7). Then, the probability of feasibility can be taken as the product of the probabilities that each component is positive, and can thus be written as the cumulative distribution function of a standard normal distribution, raised to the nth power (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 7):



Substituting this expression into Eq. (3), we obtain an extremely accurate analytical approximation of the probability of feasibility (Fig. 3, black curves): the probability p F(α) is vanishingly small when α = 0 (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 3), and increases smoothly to 1 with increasing α. Eq. (4) shows that the details of the distribution of interactions (Fig. 3, linetypes), once accounted for the correlation (Fig. 3, colors), are irrelevant when the system is large. This means that asymptotically, the curve describing the probability of feasibility is universal. Interestingly, exactly as a negative correlation between interaction strengths improves the chance of stability16, it also increases the probability of feasibility21. Contrary to current expectations14, the effect of the pairwise correlation ρ on the probability of feasibility remains significant for large systems (n = 1000 in Fig. 3). Additionally, the transition to feasibility also remains smooth compared to stability (Fig. 3, and Supplementary Fig. 10, see Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 8 for a detailed discussion) for large systems.
Importantly, our calculations show that for large systems the amount of self-regulation required for feasibility is high enough (i.e., α S < α F) to yield global stability (as argued before9,14,20,32,33). Then, a feasible system will be stable with probability 1, and thus p F(α) measures the probability of coexistence for a large, random competitive system. These results have profound implications for dynamics. Competitive GLV systems can give rise to any type of dynamics, including limit cycles (when n≥3) and chaos (n≥4)23,24. Importantly, however, non-equilibrium coexistence still requires the existence of a feasible equilibrium25. But we have seen that feasibility generically implies global stability, and therefore non-equilibrium coexistence is precluded.
When the system is not feasible, extinctions will ensue, pruning the original pool of species to a subsystem with different thresholds for feasibility and stability (Fig. 2c). As such, in principle, any type of dynamics could be observed. Next, we show that, despite the change in values of α S and α F caused by extinctions, the ordering α S < α F is maintained almost surely, provided that n is large. As a result, dynamics still converge to stable equilibria even when feasibility is not attained for the initial species pool.

Robust coexistence emerges through community dynamics
So far, we have investigated how coexistence is affected by increasing α. However, intraspecific competition models the effects of a species on itself. As such, when species are lost to extinction, the level of intraspecific competition should not be affected: the coefficients on the diagonal do not change when the matrix is pruned of the populations that have gone extinct. Thus, we turn our attention to a pool of n populations where we fix α < α S < α F (analogous to system I in Fig. 1), and consider “top-down assembly” (where all the species in the pool are introduced in the environment at the same time, Fig. 4a). Since we are below the feasibility threshold, some populations go extinct and, as a result, α F and α S changes (both values depend on n; Fig. 2c). We re-compute their values every time an extinction occurs (plotted in Fig. 4b), and find that their initial ordering is maintained throughout the dynamics until the system converges to a stable equilibrium after ecological dynamics have elapsed. Furthermore, we show (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 12) that the same equilibrium can be achieved via “bottom-up assembly”, through successive invasions26.
To confirm that these observations are a generic feature, we plot the ratio α F/α S when we run the same simulation in the previous example for many draws of random systems with the same characteristics (Fig. 4c). We see that the ratio is kept above one, implying that the relationship α S < α F is maintained throughout the dynamics for all the simulations. This shows that, with high probability, the dynamical outcome of large random competitive systems is always the same: a sub-set of the species pool will coexist robustly at an equilibrium that is characterized by α S < α F < α; the equilibrium is stable, and the last few populations to go extinct (if started in phase I), or all the extinct populations (if started in phase II) cannot re-invade the system.

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript addresses a theoretical question whether feasible equilibria in large random competitive ecological systems are also dynamically stable. Based on analytical and numerical investigations of random matrix models, the authors concluded that feasibility implied stability in large systems governed by Lotka–Volterra dynamics with random interactions. The central claim is that the transition to dynamical stability consistently precedes the transition to feasibility, thus any feasible equilibrium is necessarily stable. These results provide a plausible explanation for the empirical observations in nature that communities of organisms interacting primarily through competition—such as species at the same trophic level—often exhibit stable equilibria, whereas sustained cycles and chaotic dynamics are more commonly associated with predator-prey systems or structured populations.
We found these results mathematically elegant and conceptually important. The analytical framework and insights offered here contribute to bridging ecological theories and observations, and the paper shall stimulate further research on the mechanisms underlying ecological stability. However, we have several concerns about the presentation, generality, and robustness of the results.
(1) The definition of stability needs to be further clarified. The ecological literature covers a broad set of different definitions of stability (local stability, resistance, recovery, variability, etc.), therefore it is important to clarify the meaning of ‘stability’ in the introduction as early as possible. Reading the paper, we had been thinking about ‘local stability’, but later it turned out to be ‘global stability’ after reading Fig. 1 and line 71. We believe that it is important to clarify in the Introduction which measure of stability will be focused on, why this measure is chosen (from the broad set, as well as between global vs. local stability), how they are defined and quantified, etc. In this regard, the authors may incorporate some general discussion form the supplementary materials explaining local and global stability.
(2) The paper included many arguments that was presented as general conclusions (e.g., L28, L93, L139, L172), which however – to the best of our understanding – hold only under certain contexts. For instance, in the abstract the statement “feasible systems will necessarily be stable” (line 28) was presented as a strong conclusion, but clearly it holds only under the study context using large competitive systems with random interaction strengths. Even in this context, the argument was supported primarily by asymptotic approximations and simulations, and neither the main text nor the appendix provided formal mathematical proofs establishing that α_S<α_F holds for all random matrices within the model class. Our preliminary simulations revealed counterexamples (i.e., feasible but unstable equilibria) even for n=50. So we recommend to be more cautious with conclusions, perhaps – feasibility implies stability with high probability in large random systems. Similarly, the main text and figure captions included quite a number of strong arguments with “always” “invariably” and “necessarily”. We recommend the authors to check throughout and avoid overstatement of the generality.
(3) The robustness of the results needs more examination. The paper did not provide sufficient information on the uncertainty involved in the simulations, such as confidence intervals, failure rates, or sensitivity bounds on the probability that feasibility implies stability (e.g., Figs. 2 & 3). Without such information, it is difficult to assess how robust the results are to variation in model settings. In particular, since the analytical solutions were obtained under the assumption of large communities with random interactions, we were wondering how large (cid:1) needs to be for the asymptotic results to reach a certain precision. The bottom-left panel in Fig. 2 provided some insights into this point, but an extended investigation would be useful for understanding the behaviors of the analytical solutions.
(4) Overall, the paper was quite brief, in terms of both results and discussion. This had made additional difficulties in the understanding of the paper. We recommended the authors to expand the manuscript by adding necessary explanations (e.g., context of analyses and conclusions, as explained above) and expanding the analyses by incorporating some results from the appendix. In particular, the main text presented the solutions mainly for feasibility, but little for the global stability. Is there a solution for the latter? If so, please provide them. If not, explain how were the thresholds obtained for stability in Figs. 1 & 2 (triangles)?
Moreover, the discussion should be substantially expanded to make connections to the literature. For instance, the recent paper by Hu et al. (2022) illustrated transitions from stable & feasible coexistence, to stable and unfeasible coexistence, and to fluctuating coexistence, as the number of species and average interaction strength increased. How do the findings in the current paper relate to and differ from Hu et al. (2022)? Also, many ecological models can produce scenarios where feasible equilibrium is not stable, such as the simplest two-species model with L-V type competition. How to reconcile the present study with these cases? Again, this needs to clarify the context of the results in this paper and reconcile them with broader models and patterns under different settings in the literature.
Minor comments:
Line 42. The statement “the stability of an equilibrium requires its existence (feasibility) in the first place” did not seem correct. As an example, Fig. 1 clearly showed the case (case II) where the community was infeasible but globally stable. Please specify the context where such argument should hold.
Line 104: vague arguments. What does it mean by ‘several transitions’? Please specify it if it is important, otherwise simplify the text.
Line 147: “the levels of intraspecific competition remain more or less constant over time” – why? Environmental fluctuations can certainly lead to variation in carrying capacity (K_i) and thus intraspecific competition (as defined here, i.e., α_ii=1/K_i). We felt that this argument argument was an assumption, but presented as a conclusion. This should be clarified.
Line 206: why ‘proportional to each other’? In the equation, y* also occur in the dominator, making it nonlinear.
Fig. 1: this is a very clear and interesting illustration. We think that such transitions could (though not necessarily always) occur already in L-V models with two competitors – that is, alternative stable states at low α_ii, deterministic exclusion at higher α_ii, and coexistence at very high α_ii. If so, this may help the readers to make the bridge to existing knowledge.

### Reviewer 2

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 3

I found the work presented in ‘Robust coexistence in ecological competitive communities’ very interesting, elegantly presented and quite exciting frankly. The authors demonstrate the significance of self-regulation as a mechanism for community persistence. In particular, the authors use random matrices to generate competitive ecological communities and show that increasing self-regulation (intra-specific competition) first achieves stability (fixed point equilibrium) and then feasibility (positive density of species at equilibrium). The order of stability being attained prior to feasibility (along the self-regulation gradient) implies that feasibility guarantees stability. An important corollary of this work is that competitive communities (that are large and have randomly distributed interaction strengths, a fundamental assumption and caveat) will have stable equilibria rather than non-equilibrium steady states.
I have one comment which touches upon the basic assumptions of this work. The authors use a single value for self-regulation, alpha, across species. Do I understand this correctly? This scenario would imply that all species share the same strength of self-regulation, while the strength of inter-specific interactions can vary. I wonder what would happen if there was a mean alpha for a matrix, rather than a fixed alpha for all species? How strongly would this impact the insights (obviously given different assumptions about the distribution of alpha’s)? Adding to this, what would happen if these alpha values were somehow correlated to the inter-specific interaction terms? For instance, a weak competitor with respect to other species, would presumably also have weak self-regulation to increase its survival chances. I understand that the authors simplified a very complex problem and I appreciate the value in such an approach. However, since the fundamental ecological parameter studied here is self-regulation, I would like the authors to explore the limitations of their simplifying assumptions regarding this parameter. Ultimately, it is important to understand the generality of their results to relaxing this assumption.
Besides this and to the extent that I was able to follow the mathematical analyses in the supplement, I found the justification of the results persuasive. Moreover, I liked how the manuscript was written; concisely, clearly and with a linearly progressing narrative. Overall, I really enjoyed reading this study and I would be happy to see it published so as to stimulate a debate in the broader community of interested ecologists.
My only regret was the absence of an ecological interpretation for the results, beyond the very obvious statements. For instance, as I mention in a comment below, I see some relation of certain results to niche theory; it would be very insightful to link the two. I believe there’s plenty of scope to expand on such nuances in the manuscript and I feel the authors would be doing ecologist readers a great service to expand on this aspect. Ultimately, given the journal and the style of the manuscript, I view this suggestion more as a ‘nice to have’ than a requirement for publication.

The final sentence is quite strong. The absence of non-equilibrium steady states rests on certain assumptions (large, random interaction matrices). l.124-127 & eq. (4): it appears that as n increases, only the correlation (rho) will impact the variance and hence the probability of feasibility. If that is the case, I am not sure I understand l. 125, where I perceive the message as being that correlation (besides the mean and variance of the interaction matrix) is irrelevant.
l.131 e.g., what does P_F=0.5 mean for a community? In other words, what determines whether or not a community will be feasible? Are there other aspects of the interaction matrix distribution (higher moments?) whose consideration will make this outcome more definite? ## Introduction

The notions of intraspecific competition and population self-regulation play a central role in ecological theory, leading to foundational concepts such as limiting similarity and niche differentiation1–6. They also are crucial for coexistence: for example, May7 showed that ecological dynamics can be stabilized by imposing sufficiently strong intraspecific competition, and that for large systems with random species interactions the stability transition is universal (independent of the probability distribution used to model interactions) and sharp (always achieved at the same critical value of intraspecific competition). Importantly, the existence of an equilibrium (feasibility) is a necessary condition for coexistence. Further, results on stability can dramatically change when accounting for feasibility. The first contribution to this problem can be traced back to a response to May’s work on stability8, showing that in competitive Lotka-Volterra models with random interactions the probability of stability, conditioned on the presence of a feasible equilibrium, does increase, rather than decrease with system size. Since then, significant advances have been gradually accumulating in the literature9–15 (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 2). However, the progress on the study of feasibility has yet to match that reached for stability7,16–18. Here we show that accounting for feasibility is key to determining the expected dynamics of large competitive systems.

We compute the probability that a system would display a feasible equilibrium given its level of intraspecific competition, size, and the statistics on the random distribution of species interactions. We show that the transition to feasibility is universal, as for stability, but is not sharp—thereby extending, generalizing and refining previous results8,9,12,14,19–22. More importantly, we show that, in large competitive systems, when we increase the strength of intraspecific competition, the transition to stability precedes that to feasibility8,9,20. Therefore, in these large systems feasibility implies stability. This result holds even when the initial pool of species cannot coexist, and extinctions ensue. That is, during ecological dynamics, species extinctions will alter the values for the stability and feasibility thresholds, but not their ordering. Differently from May, who focused on local asymptotic stability of an equilibrium, here we consider the stronger criterion of global stability—robust coexistence in which populations rebound from any perturbation short of extinction.

Overall, these findings have far-reaching implications for the ecological dynamics of large random competitive ecosystems. They rule out coexistence through limit cycles or chaos23,24, and instead indicate that the community dynamics converge to a highly-robust equilibrium, such that (1) any perturbation short of extinction would be buffered, (2) the community resists invasions, and (3) it can be assembled from the ground up25,26.

(1) has a feasible (i.e., biologically attainable) equilibrium whenever there is a x⋆ > 0 such that x_ i = 0 for all populations, and that such a feasible equilibrium is asymptotically stable if dynamics return to it following a perturbation.
Following May7, we model A as the sum of two matrices, A = αI + B, where B collects the inter-specific interactions (B ij, i≠j). I is the identity random matrix, and α ≥ 0 the intraspecific competition in the system, assumed to be the same for all species (relaxing this assumption does not change the results, see Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 9).
Now we consider increasing α from zero to an arbitrary large positive value, and track the effects of this change on coexistence. We denote α S as the level of intraspecific competition that is sufficient to guarantee the (global) stability of an equilibrium (Methods, and Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3). Importantly, for any α ≥ α S stability is maintained, i.e., once surpassed this threshold, dynamics always converge to a globally stable equilibrium. Here we ask whether, in analogy to stability, there exist a critical level α F that a) guarantees the existence of a positive equilibrium, and b) further increasing α ≥ α F retains the feasibility of the equilibrium. In particular, we want to probe the relationship between α F and α S.
We start with a toy example (Fig. 1, n = 6, see Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Fig. 3 for an example with two populations), illustrating the effect of increasing α on feasibility and stability. We first sample a baseline interaction matrix B, and compute the thresholds for stability, α S, and feasibility, α F (Methods, and Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3, and Supplementary Note 2, Sec. 4), marked in Fig. 1 with green and yellow triangles, respectively. We then construct three interaction matrices A that differ only in their intraspecific competition values, α I, α II, and α III (Fig. 1). For each system, we integrate the dynamics in Eq. (1) from two different initial conditions (Fig. 1 bottom panels, solid vs. dashed lines), revealing three qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes.
System I (Fig. 1, left) undergoes extinctions and displays alternative stable states, indicating that the coexistence equilibrium is not feasible, and the resulting sub-community equilibrium is not globally stable (indeed, neither stability nor feasibility thresholds have been surpassed, since α I < α S < α F). System II (Fig. 1, middle), also displays extinctions (as there is no feasible equilibrium), but starting from different initial conditions no longer leads to different outcomes, because the equilibrium of the sub-community is globally stable (α S < α II < α F, and see Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3). Finally, system III (Fig. 1, right), exhibits all populations coexisting stably (α S < α F < α III). From this single realization, we can see that stability is achieved before feasibility. Next, we show that this is the case for large random ecological communities (but see Supplementary Note 2, Sec. 3 for results on small or arbitrary competitive systems).

Feasibility implies robust coexistence almost surely
As long as populations are statistically equivalent (i.e., there is no a priori structure making some populations behave differently from the rest), the distribution of the equilibrium values, y⋆, has always the same mean and correlation structure (Methods). Moreover, when n is large, we can assume the components of y⋆ to be approximately normally distributed9 and uncorrelated (“Methods”, and Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 7). Then, the probability of feasibility can be taken as the product of the probabilities that each component is positive, and can thus be written as the cumulative distribution function of a standard normal distribution, raised to the nth power (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 7):



Substituting this expression into Eq. (3), we obtain an extremely accurate analytical approximation of the probability of feasibility (Fig. 3, black curves): the probability p F(α) is vanishingly small when α = 0 (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 3), and increases smoothly to 1 with increasing α. Eq. (4) shows that the details of the distribution of interactions (Fig. 3, linetypes), once accounted for the correlation (Fig. 3, colors), are irrelevant when the system is large. This means that asymptotically, the curve describing the probability of feasibility is universal. Interestingly, exactly as a negative correlation between interaction strengths improves the chance of stability16, it also increases the probability of feasibility21. Contrary to current expectations14, the effect of the pairwise correlation ρ on the probability of feasibility remains significant for large systems (n = 1000 in Fig. 3). Additionally, the transition to feasibility also remains smooth compared to stability (Fig. 3, and Supplementary Fig. 10, see Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 8 for a detailed discussion) for large systems.
Importantly, our calculations show that for large systems the amount of self-regulation required for feasibility is high enough (i.e., α S < α F) to yield global stability (as argued before9,14,20,32,33). Then, a feasible system will be stable with probability 1, and thus p F(α) measures the probability of coexistence for a large, random competitive system. These results have profound implications for dynamics. Competitive GLV systems can give rise to any type of dynamics, including limit cycles (when n≥3) and chaos (n≥4)23,24. Importantly, however, non-equilibrium coexistence still requires the existence of a feasible equilibrium25. But we have seen that feasibility generically implies global stability, and therefore non-equilibrium coexistence is precluded.
When the system is not feasible, extinctions will ensue, pruning the original pool of species to a subsystem with different thresholds for feasibility and stability (Fig. 2c). As such, in principle, any type of dynamics could be observed. Next, we show that, despite the change in values of α S and α F caused by extinctions, the ordering α S < α F is maintained almost surely, provided that n is large. As a result, dynamics still converge to stable equilibria even when feasibility is not attained for the initial species pool.

Robust coexistence emerges through community dynamics
So far, we have investigated how coexistence is affected by increasing α. However, intraspecific competition models the effects of a species on itself. As such, when species are lost to extinction, the level of intraspecific competition should not be affected: the coefficients on the diagonal do not change when the matrix is pruned of the populations that have gone extinct. Thus, we turn our attention to a pool of n populations where we fix α < α S < α F (analogous to system I in Fig. 1), and consider “top-down assembly” (where all the species in the pool are introduced in the environment at the same time, Fig. 4a). Since we are below the feasibility threshold, some populations go extinct and, as a result, α F and α S changes (both values depend on n; Fig. 2c). We re-compute their values every time an extinction occurs (plotted in Fig. 4b), and find that their initial ordering is maintained throughout the dynamics until the system converges to a stable equilibrium after ecological dynamics have elapsed. Furthermore, we show (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 12) that the same equilibrium can be achieved via “bottom-up assembly”, through successive invasions26.
To confirm that these observations are a generic feature, we plot the ratio α F/α S when we run the same simulation in the previous example for many draws of random systems with the same characteristics (Fig. 4c). We see that the ratio is kept above one, implying that the relationship α S < α F is maintained throughout the dynamics for all the simulations. This shows that, with high probability, the dynamical outcome of large random competitive systems is always the same: a sub-set of the species pool will coexist robustly at an equilibrium that is characterized by α S < α F < α; the equilibrium is stable, and the last few populations to go extinct (if started in phase I), or all the extinct populations (if started in phase II) cannot re-invade the system.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript addresses a theoretical question whether feasible equilibria in large random competitive ecological systems are also dynamically stable. Based on analytical and numerical investigations of random matrix models, the authors concluded that feasibility implied stability in large systems governed by Lotka–Volterra dynamics with random interactions. The central claim is that the transition to dynamical stability consistently precedes the transition to feasibility, thus any feasible equilibrium is necessarily stable. These results provide a plausible explanation for the empirical observations in nature that communities of organisms interacting primarily through competition—such as species at the same trophic level—often exhibit stable equilibria, whereas sustained cycles and chaotic dynamics are more commonly associated with predator-prey systems or structured populations.
We found these results mathematically elegant and conceptually important. The analytical framework and insights offered here contribute to bridging ecological theories and observations, and the paper shall stimulate further research on the mechanisms underlying ecological stability. However, we have several concerns about the presentation, generality, and robustness of the results.
(1) The definition of stability needs to be further clarified. The ecological literature covers a broad set of different definitions of stability (local stability, resistance, recovery, variability, etc.), therefore it is important to clarify the meaning of ‘stability’ in the introduction as early as possible. Reading the paper, we had been thinking about ‘local stability’, but later it turned out to be ‘global stability’ after reading Fig. 1 and line 71. We believe that it is important to clarify in the Introduction which measure of stability will be focused on, why this measure is chosen (from the broad set, as well as between global vs. local stability), how they are defined and quantified, etc. In this regard, the authors may incorporate some general discussion form the supplementary materials explaining local and global stability.
(2) The paper included many arguments that was presented as general conclusions (e.g., L28, L93, L139, L172), which however – to the best of our understanding – hold only under certain contexts. For instance, in the abstract the statement “feasible systems will necessarily be stable” (line 28) was presented as a strong conclusion, but clearly it holds only under the study context using large competitive systems with random interaction strengths. Even in this context, the argument was supported primarily by asymptotic approximations and simulations, and neither the main text nor the appendix provided formal mathematical proofs establishing that α_S<α_F holds for all random matrices within the model class. Our preliminary simulations revealed counterexamples (i.e., feasible but unstable equilibria) even for n=50. So we recommend to be more cautious with conclusions, perhaps – feasibility implies stability with high probability in large random systems. Similarly, the main text and figure captions included quite a number of strong arguments with “always” “invariably” and “necessarily”. We recommend the authors to check throughout and avoid overstatement of the generality.
(3) The robustness of the results needs more examination. The paper did not provide sufficient information on the uncertainty involved in the simulations, such as confidence intervals, failure rates, or sensitivity bounds on the probability that feasibility implies stability (e.g., Figs. 2 & 3). Without such information, it is difficult to assess how robust the results are to variation in model settings. In particular, since the analytical solutions were obtained under the assumption of large communities with random interactions, we were wondering how large (cid:1) needs to be for the asymptotic results to reach a certain precision. The bottom-left panel in Fig. 2 provided some insights into this point, but an extended investigation would be useful for understanding the behaviors of the analytical solutions.
(4) Overall, the paper was quite brief, in terms of both results and discussion. This had made additional difficulties in the understanding of the paper. We recommended the authors to expand the manuscript by adding necessary explanations (e.g., context of analyses and conclusions, as explained above) and expanding the analyses by incorporating some results from the appendix. In particular, the main text presented the solutions mainly for feasibility, but little for the global stability. Is there a solution for the latter? If so, please provide them. If not, explain how were the thresholds obtained for stability in Figs. 1 & 2 (triangles)?
Moreover, the discussion should be substantially expanded to make connections to the literature. For instance, the recent paper by Hu et al. (2022) illustrated transitions from stable & feasible coexistence, to stable and unfeasible coexistence, and to fluctuating coexistence, as the number of species and average interaction strength increased. How do the findings in the current paper relate to and differ from Hu et al. (2022)? Also, many ecological models can produce scenarios where feasible equilibrium is not stable, such as the simplest two-species model with L-V type competition. How to reconcile the present study with these cases? Again, this needs to clarify the context of the results in this paper and reconcile them with broader models and patterns under different settings in the literature.

### Reviewer 3

I found the work presented in ‘Robust coexistence in ecological competitive communities’ very interesting, elegantly presented and quite exciting frankly. The authors demonstrate the significance of self-regulation as a mechanism for community persistence. In particular, the authors use random matrices to generate competitive ecological communities and show that increasing self-regulation (intra-specific competition) first achieves stability (fixed point equilibrium) and then feasibility (positive density of species at equilibrium). The order of stability being attained prior to feasibility (along the self-regulation gradient) implies that feasibility guarantees stability. An important corollary of this work is that competitive communities (that are large and have randomly distributed interaction strengths, a fundamental assumption and caveat) will have stable equilibria rather than non-equilibrium steady states.
I have one comment which touches upon the basic assumptions of this work. The authors use a single value for self-regulation, alpha, across species. Do I understand this correctly? This scenario would imply that all species share the same strength of self-regulation, while the strength of inter-specific interactions can vary. I wonder what would happen if there was a mean alpha for a matrix, rather than a fixed alpha for all species? How strongly would this impact the insights (obviously given different assumptions about the distribution of alpha’s)? Adding to this, what would happen if these alpha values were somehow correlated to the inter-specific interaction terms? For instance, a weak competitor with respect to other species, would presumably also have weak self-regulation to increase its survival chances. I understand that the authors simplified a very complex problem and I appreciate the value in such an approach. However, since the fundamental ecological parameter studied here is self-regulation, I would like the authors to explore the limitations of their simplifying assumptions regarding this parameter. Ultimately, it is important to understand the generality of their results to relaxing this assumption.
Besides this and to the extent that I was able to follow the mathematical analyses in the supplement, I found the justification of the results persuasive. Moreover, I liked how the manuscript was written; concisely, clearly and with a linearly progressing narrative. Overall, I really enjoyed reading this study and I would be happy to see it published so as to stimulate a debate in the broader community of interested ecologists.
My only regret was the absence of an ecological interpretation for the results, beyond the very obvious statements. I believe there’s plenty of scope to expand on such nuances in the manuscript and I feel the authors would be doing ecologist readers a great service to expand on this aspect. Ultimately, given the journal and the style of the manuscript, I view this suggestion more as a ‘nice to have’ than a requirement for publication.

## Paper

## Abstract

Darwin already recognized that competition is fiercest among conspecifics, a principle that later made intraspecific competition central to ecological theory through concepts such as niche differentiation and limiting similarity. Beyond shaping coexistence, strong intraspecific competition can also stabilize community dynamics by ensuring that populations return to equilibrium after disturbance. Here we investigate a more fundamental question: how intraspecific competition influences the very existence of a steady state (feasibility) in large random ecological communities dominated by competition. We show that, in analogy with classical results on stability, there is a critical level of intraspecific competition above which a feasible steady state is guaranteed to exist. We derive a general expression for the probability of feasibility and prove that, asymptotically (as species number grows), the transition to stability occurs before the transition to feasibility with probability one. Thus, in large competitive communities, any feasible equilibrium is automatically stable. This ordering persists even when many species in the initial pool cannot coexist and extinctions occur: the dynamics prune the community, shifting feasibility and stability thresholds but never reversing their order. These results imply that large competitive communities generically converge to a globally stable equilibrium, making sustained oscillations or chaos unlikely—consistent with experimental observations.

## Introduction

The notions of intraspecific competition and population self-regulation play a central role in ecological theory, leading to foundational concepts such as limiting similarity and niche differentiation1–6. They also are crucial for coexistence: for example, May7 showed that ecological dynamics can be stabilized by imposing sufficiently strong intraspecific competition, and that for large systems with random species interactions the stability transition is universal (independent of the probability distribution used to model interactions) and sharp (always achieved at the same critical value of intraspecific competition). Importantly, the existence of an equilibrium (feasibility) is a necessary condition for coexistence. Further, results on stability can dramatically change when accounting for feasibility. The first contribution to this problem can be traced back to a response to May’s work on stability8, showing that in competitive Lotka-Volterra models with random interactions the probability of stability, conditioned on the presence of a feasible equilibrium, does increase, rather than decrease with system size. Since then, significant advances have been gradually accumulating in the literature9–15 (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 2). However, the progress on the study of feasibility has yet to match that reached for stability7,16–18. Here we show that accounting for feasibility is key to determining the expected dynamics of large competitive systems.

We compute the probability that a system would display a feasible equilibrium given its level of intraspecific competition, size, and the statistics on the random distribution of species interactions. We show that the transition to feasibility is universal, as for stability, but is not sharp—thereby extending, generalizing and refining previous results8,9,12,14,19–22. More importantly, we show that, in large competitive systems, when we increase the strength of intraspecific competition, the transition to stability precedes that to feasibility8,9,20. Therefore, in these large systems feasibility implies stability. This result holds even when the initial pool of species cannot coexist, and extinctions ensue. That is, during ecological dynamics, species extinctions will alter the values for the stability and feasibility thresholds, but not their ordering. Differently from May, who focused on local asymptotic stability of an equilibrium, here we consider the stronger criterion of global stability—robust coexistence in which populations rebound from any perturbation short of extinction.

Overall, these findings have far-reaching implications for the ecological dynamics of large random competitive ecosystems. They rule out coexistence through limit cycles or chaos23,24, and instead indicate that the community dynamics converge to a highly-robust equilibrium, such that (1) any perturbation short of extinction would be buffered, (2) the community resists invasions, and (3) it can be assembled from the ground up25,26.
