Following May7, we model A as the sum of two matrices, A = αI + B, where B collects the inter-specific interactions (B ij, i≠j). I is the identity random matrix, and α ≥ 0 the intraspecific competition in the system, assumed to be the same for all species (relaxing this assumption does not change the results, see Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 9).
Now we consider increasing α from zero to an arbitrary large positive value, and track the effects of this change on coexistence. We denote α S as the level of intraspecific competition that is sufficient to guarantee the (global) stability of an equilibrium (Methods, and Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3). Importantly, for any α ≥ α S stability is maintained, i.e., once surpassed this threshold, dynamics always converge to a globally stable equilibrium. Here we ask whether, in analogy to stability, there exist a critical level α F that a) guarantees the existence of a positive equilibrium, and b) further increasing α ≥ α F retains the feasibility of the equilibrium. In particular, we want to probe the relationship between α F and α S.
We start with a toy example (Fig. 1, n = 6, see Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Fig. 3 for an example with two populations), illustrating the effect of increasing α on feasibility and stability. We first sample a baseline interaction matrix B, and compute the thresholds for stability, α S, and feasibility, α F (Methods, and Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3, and Supplementary Note 2, Sec. 4), marked in Fig. 1 with green and yellow triangles, respectively. We then construct three interaction matrices A that differ only in their intraspecific competition values, α I, α II, and α III (Fig. 1). For each system, we integrate the dynamics in Eq. (1) from two different initial conditions (Fig. 1 bottom panels, solid vs. dashed lines), revealing three qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes.
System I (Fig. 1, left) undergoes extinctions and displays alternative stable states, indicating that the coexistence equilibrium is not feasible, and the resulting sub-community equilibrium is not globally stable (indeed, neither stability nor feasibility thresholds have been surpassed, since α I < α S < α F). System II (Fig. 1, middle), also displays extinctions (as there is no feasible equilibrium), but starting from different initial conditions no longer leads to different outcomes, because the equilibrium of the sub-community is globally stable (α S < α II < α F, and see Supplementary Note 1, Sec. 3). Finally, system III (Fig. 1, right), exhibits all populations coexisting stably (α S < α F < α III). From this single realization, we can see that stability is achieved before feasibility. Next, we show that this is the case for large random ecological communities (but see Supplementary Note 2, Sec. 3 for results on small or arbitrary competitive systems).

Feasibility implies robust coexistence almost surely
As long as populations are statistically equivalent (i.e., there is no a priori structure making some populations behave differently from the rest), the distribution of the equilibrium values, y⋆, has always the same mean and correlation structure (Methods). Moreover, when n is large, we can assume the components of y⋆ to be approximately normally distributed9 and uncorrelated (“Methods”, and Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 7). Then, the probability of feasibility can be taken as the product of the probabilities that each component is positive, and can thus be written as the cumulative distribution function of a standard normal distribution, raised to the nth power (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 7):



Substituting this expression into Eq. (3), we obtain an extremely accurate analytical approximation of the probability of feasibility (Fig. 3, black curves): the probability p F(α) is vanishingly small when α = 0 (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 3), and increases smoothly to 1 with increasing α. Eq. (4) shows that the details of the distribution of interactions (Fig. 3, linetypes), once accounted for the correlation (Fig. 3, colors), are irrelevant when the system is large. This means that asymptotically, the curve describing the probability of feasibility is universal. Interestingly, exactly as a negative correlation between interaction strengths improves the chance of stability16, it also increases the probability of feasibility21. Contrary to current expectations14, the effect of the pairwise correlation ρ on the probability of feasibility remains significant for large systems (n = 1000 in Fig. 3). Additionally, the transition to feasibility also remains smooth compared to stability (Fig. 3, and Supplementary Fig. 10, see Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 8 for a detailed discussion) for large systems.
Importantly, our calculations show that for large systems the amount of self-regulation required for feasibility is high enough (i.e., α S < α F) to yield global stability (as argued before9,14,20,32,33). Then, a feasible system will be stable with probability 1, and thus p F(α) measures the probability of coexistence for a large, random competitive system. These results have profound implications for dynamics. Competitive GLV systems can give rise to any type of dynamics, including limit cycles (when n≥3) and chaos (n≥4)23,24. Importantly, however, non-equilibrium coexistence still requires the existence of a feasible equilibrium25. But we have seen that feasibility generically implies global stability, and therefore non-equilibrium coexistence is precluded.
When the system is not feasible, extinctions will ensue, pruning the original pool of species to a subsystem with different thresholds for feasibility and stability (Fig. 2c). As such, in principle, any type of dynamics could be observed. Next, we show that, despite the change in values of α S and α F caused by extinctions, the ordering α S < α F is maintained almost surely, provided that n is large. As a result, dynamics still converge to stable equilibria even when feasibility is not attained for the initial species pool.

Robust coexistence emerges through community dynamics
So far, we have investigated how coexistence is affected by increasing α. However, intraspecific competition models the effects of a species on itself. As such, when species are lost to extinction, the level of intraspecific competition should not be affected: the coefficients on the diagonal do not change when the matrix is pruned of the populations that have gone extinct. Thus, we turn our attention to a pool of n populations where we fix α < α S < α F (analogous to system I in Fig. 1), and consider “top-down assembly” (where all the species in the pool are introduced in the environment at the same time, Fig. 4a). Since we are below the feasibility threshold, some populations go extinct and, as a result, α F and α S changes (both values depend on n; Fig. 2c). We re-compute their values every time an extinction occurs (plotted in Fig. 4b), and find that their initial ordering is maintained throughout the dynamics until the system converges to a stable equilibrium after ecological dynamics have elapsed. Furthermore, we show (Supplementary Note 3, Sec. 12) that the same equilibrium can be achieved via “bottom-up assembly”, through successive invasions26.
To confirm that these observations are a generic feature, we plot the ratio α F/α S when we run the same simulation in the previous example for many draws of random systems with the same characteristics (Fig. 4c). We see that the ratio is kept above one, implying that the relationship α S < α F is maintained throughout the dynamics for all the simulations. This shows that, with high probability, the dynamical outcome of large random competitive systems is always the same: a sub-set of the species pool will coexist robustly at an equilibrium that is characterized by α S < α F < α; the equilibrium is stable, and the last few populations to go extinct (if started in phase I), or all the extinct populations (if started in phase II) cannot re-invade the system.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript addresses a theoretical question whether feasible equilibria in large random competitive ecological systems are also dynamically stable. Based on analytical and numerical investigations of random matrix models, the authors concluded that feasibility implied stability in large systems governed by Lotka–Volterra dynamics with random interactions. The central claim is that the transition to dynamical stability consistently precedes the transition to feasibility, thus any feasible equilibrium is necessarily stable. These results provide a plausible explanation for the empirical observations in nature that communities of organisms interacting primarily through competition—such as species at the same trophic level—often exhibit stable equilibria, whereas sustained cycles and chaotic dynamics are more commonly associated with predator-prey systems or structured populations.
We found these results mathematically elegant and conceptually important. The analytical framework and insights offered here contribute to bridging ecological theories and observations, and the paper shall stimulate further research on the mechanisms underlying ecological stability. However, we have several concerns about the presentation, generality, and robustness of the results.
(1) The definition of stability needs to be further clarified. The ecological literature covers a broad set of different definitions of stability (local stability, resistance, recovery, variability, etc.), therefore it is important to clarify the meaning of ‘stability’ in the introduction as early as possible. Reading the paper, we had been thinking about ‘local stability’, but later it turned out to be ‘global stability’ after reading Fig. 1 and line 71. We believe that it is important to clarify in the Introduction which measure of stability will be focused on, why this measure is chosen (from the broad set, as well as between global vs. local stability), how they are defined and quantified, etc. In this regard, the authors may incorporate some general discussion form the supplementary materials explaining local and global stability.
(2) The paper included many arguments that was presented as general conclusions (e.g., L28, L93, L139, L172), which however – to the best of our understanding – hold only under certain contexts. For instance, in the abstract the statement “feasible systems will necessarily be stable” (line 28) was presented as a strong conclusion, but clearly it holds only under the study context using large competitive systems with random interaction strengths. Even in this context, the argument was supported primarily by asymptotic approximations and simulations, and neither the main text nor the appendix provided formal mathematical proofs establishing that α_S<α_F holds for all random matrices within the model class. Our preliminary simulations revealed counterexamples (i.e., feasible but unstable equilibria) even for n=50. So we recommend to be more cautious with conclusions, perhaps – feasibility implies stability with high probability in large random systems. Similarly, the main text and figure captions included quite a number of strong arguments with “always” “invariably” and “necessarily”. We recommend the authors to check throughout and avoid overstatement of the generality.
(3) The robustness of the results needs more examination. The paper did not provide sufficient information on the uncertainty involved in the simulations, such as confidence intervals, failure rates, or sensitivity bounds on the probability that feasibility implies stability (e.g., Figs. 2 & 3). Without such information, it is difficult to assess how robust the results are to variation in model settings. In particular, since the analytical solutions were obtained under the assumption of large communities with random interactions, we were wondering how large (cid:1) needs to be for the asymptotic results to reach a certain precision. The bottom-left panel in Fig. 2 provided some insights into this point, but an extended investigation would be useful for understanding the behaviors of the analytical solutions.
(4) Overall, the paper was quite brief, in terms of both results and discussion. This had made additional difficulties in the understanding of the paper. We recommended the authors to expand the manuscript by adding necessary explanations (e.g., context of analyses and conclusions, as explained above) and expanding the analyses by incorporating some results from the appendix. In particular, the main text presented the solutions mainly for feasibility, but little for the global stability. Is there a solution for the latter? If so, please provide them. If not, explain how were the thresholds obtained for stability in Figs. 1 & 2 (triangles)?
Moreover, the discussion should be substantially expanded to make connections to the literature. For instance, the recent paper by Hu et al. (2022) illustrated transitions from stable & feasible coexistence, to stable and unfeasible coexistence, and to fluctuating coexistence, as the number of species and average interaction strength increased. How do the findings in the current paper relate to and differ from Hu et al. (2022)? Also, many ecological models can produce scenarios where feasible equilibrium is not stable, such as the simplest two-species model with L-V type competition. How to reconcile the present study with these cases? Again, this needs to clarify the context of the results in this paper and reconcile them with broader models and patterns under different settings in the literature.

### Reviewer 3

I found the work presented in ‘Robust coexistence in ecological competitive communities’ very interesting, elegantly presented and quite exciting frankly. The authors demonstrate the significance of self-regulation as a mechanism for community persistence. In particular, the authors use random matrices to generate competitive ecological communities and show that increasing self-regulation (intra-specific competition) first achieves stability (fixed point equilibrium) and then feasibility (positive density of species at equilibrium). The order of stability being attained prior to feasibility (along the self-regulation gradient) implies that feasibility guarantees stability. An important corollary of this work is that competitive communities (that are large and have randomly distributed interaction strengths, a fundamental assumption and caveat) will have stable equilibria rather than non-equilibrium steady states.
I have one comment which touches upon the basic assumptions of this work. The authors use a single value for self-regulation, alpha, across species. Do I understand this correctly? This scenario would imply that all species share the same strength of self-regulation, while the strength of inter-specific interactions can vary. I wonder what would happen if there was a mean alpha for a matrix, rather than a fixed alpha for all species? How strongly would this impact the insights (obviously given different assumptions about the distribution of alpha’s)? Adding to this, what would happen if these alpha values were somehow correlated to the inter-specific interaction terms? For instance, a weak competitor with respect to other species, would presumably also have weak self-regulation to increase its survival chances. I understand that the authors simplified a very complex problem and I appreciate the value in such an approach. However, since the fundamental ecological parameter studied here is self-regulation, I would like the authors to explore the limitations of their simplifying assumptions regarding this parameter.
